summary: Range lights of 1897 on Plum Island that lined ships up for Death's Door; the iron rear tower still stands in a wildlife refuge, its lens now in a Gills Rock museum.

lens.where: Door County Maritime Museum northern site, Gills Rock

access.note: Island is a US Fish and Wildlife Service refuge; grounds, dwelling and tower closed; tower visible from the Northport-Washington Island ferry.

notes_for_editor: Moderate evidence. Sources disagree on: front lens order (LHF sixth, NRHP fifth); brick quantity (LHB 82,000 hauled by report date, LHF 164,000); lane length (LHB 1,600 ft, NRHP 1,650 ft); automation year (see resolved_conflicts); the NRHP 2010 says original lens still in use, LHF says removed 2015 (a later event, only LHF found; Friends of Plum and Pilot Facebook snippet in search results agrees but was not read). Light-House Board report pages (1892, 1895, 1897) were not page-verified; the 1897 volume is labelled 1896-1897 and its Plum Island passage mentions May 1897, so it is the report for fiscal year ended 30 June 1897. The 175-hour siren figure covers only 1 May to 30 June 1897. Roster stints parsed from the USLHS page; USCG crews 1950-64 kept as 'other'. Front-range record lacks its own keepers (USLHS front record has none). No newspapers were read (the single Chronicling America search timed out). LHF's account of the 1904 log entry is second-hand (cited to LHF). Record position (45.3038,-86.9549) differs from LHF (45.30769,-86.95817) and USLHS (45.3000,-86.9500); not proposed as a correction.
